categories.label: Breach of contract (goods or services)
categories.description: You had an agreement with someone to buy or supply goods or services — written, spoken, or shown by what you both did — and they didn't deliver, delivered something defective or late, or didn't pay.

generalGates.description: Hard cap on SCT claim value at 30000.
generalGates.question: How much are you claiming, in Singapore dollars?
generalGates.plainExplanation: The Small Claims Tribunals can only hear claims up to S$30,000, and only above S$20,000 if both parties agree in writing. Claims above S$30,000 must go to another court.
generalGates.missingMessage: Roughly how much money are you asking the other party to pay you?

source.title: Small Claims Tribunals Act 1984
source.provision: s 5 (prescribed limit)

generalGates.description: Pairs with gen_claim_amount_max: between S$20k and S$30k the claim is CONDITIONAL on the other party's written consent.
generalGates.question: How much are you claiming, in Singapore dollars?
generalGates.plainExplanation: Claims between S$20,000 and S$30,000 can only be heard at the Small Claims Tribunals if the other party agrees in writing to the higher limit.
generalGates.missingMessage: Roughly how much money are you asking the other party to pay you?

source.title: Small Claims Tribunals Act 1984
source.provision: s 5 (consent to higher limit)

generalGates.description: Claim must be brought within the SCT limitation period.
generalGates.question: Did the events you are claiming about happen within the last 2 years?
generalGates.plainExplanation: A claim must be filed at the Small Claims Tribunals within 2 years of the date the dispute arose. Older disputes cannot be heard there.
generalGates.missingMessage: When did the problem first happen — for example, when was the payment due, or when did you receive the faulty goods?

source.title: Small Claims Tribunals Act 1984
source.provision: limitation period

categoryGates.description: Proof of Agreement. onFail FAIL because with no agreement of any kind there is no contract claim — legal to confirm severity.
categoryGates.question: Do you have proof of an agreement between you and the other party — written, oral, or based on conduct (e.g. payment made, goods delivered)?

options.label: Written — a contract, messages, emails or a document
Oral — I can say who agreed what, and when
By conduct — e.g. an invoice was sent and paid, or goods were delivered
There was no identifiable agreement of any kind

categoryGates.plainExplanation: Contracts don't need to be written to be enforceable in Singapore, except specific categories (real property, guarantees). Oral and implied contracts are equally valid, but harder to evidence.
categoryGates.missingMessage: Did money change hands, was anything delivered, or did you exchange any messages or receipts confirming what was agreed?
categoryGates.exceptions: A contract can form through conduct alone. Contracts for the sale or lease of land, and guarantees, must be in writing under the Civil Law Act — flag if the claim touches these.

source.title: Civil Law Act 1909; general common law of contract formation
source.provision: Civil Law Act 1909 (writing requirements for specific contracts)

categoryGates.description: Subject Matter — what was to be delivered/performed. Table says 'claim may fail for uncertainty'; set WEAKNESS so the tool probes rather than stops — legal to confirm.
categoryGates.question: Can you describe exactly what the other party agreed to deliver or perform — for example the make and model, or the scope of work?
categoryGates.plainExplanation: Establishes the contract's subject matter, which determines which statutory implied terms apply (Sale of Goods Act for goods; general contract and tort principles for services).
categoryGates.missingMessage: Can you describe exactly what was being sold, or what work was being done?
categoryGates.exceptions: If the agreement was for a class of goods or services (e.g. 'a laptop suitable for gaming') rather than a specific item, the implied 'fitness for purpose' term becomes more central than an exact-match description term.

source.title: Sale of Goods Act 1979
source.provision: ss 13–15 (description, quality, fitness for purpose)

categoryGates.description: Consideration. onFail FAIL because no consideration suggests no binding contract (a gift, not a bargain) — legal to confirm severity.
categoryGates.question: Was a price, or something else of value in exchange, clearly agreed?
categoryGates.plainExplanation: Consideration — something of value exchanged — is a basic requirement for contract formation under Singapore law.
categoryGates.missingMessage: What was the buyer supposed to give in return — money, goods, or something else?
categoryGates.exceptions: Consideration doesn't have to be money — goods, services, or a promise all count; barter arrangements are still valid contracts.

source.title: General contract law
source.provision: Requirement of consideration

categoryGates.description: Timing — date or timeframe for delivery/performance.
categoryGates.question: Was a specific date or timeframe agreed for delivery or performance?

options.label: Yes — an exact date
Yes — a calculable timeframe, e.g. 'within 2 weeks of payment'
No date or timeframe was agreed

categoryGates.plainExplanation: Time of performance affects when breach occurs. If no date was fixed, the law implies performance within a 'reasonable time' — that is not automatically a bar to a claim, but it is harder to show delay.
categoryGates.missingMessage: Did either party mention a deadline, or was anything said about how soon this would be done?
categoryGates.exceptions: If no date was fixed, the law implies performance must occur within a 'reasonable time', assessed by trade norms and context.

source.title: Sale of Goods Act 1979
source.provision: s 29 (time of delivery); general contract law on implied reasonable time

categoryGates.description: Timing — interim milestones. Table treats absence as 'not a weakness' (evidentiary only). Draft: informational, legal to decide whether it should be a gate at all.
categoryGates.question: Were any intermediate deadlines or milestones agreed (e.g. deposit by a date, progress updates)?
categoryGates.plainExplanation: Interim milestones help establish a pattern of breach or reasonable reliance, useful for showing when things started going wrong.
categoryGates.missingMessage: Was anything supposed to happen at any point before the final delivery or completion?
categoryGates.exceptions: Absence of interim milestones doesn't affect the main claim unless one was expressly linked to a right (e.g. 'deposit due within 7 days or contract voidable').

source.title: General contract law
source.provision: Evidentiary factor, not a separate statutory obligation

categoryGates.description: Quality & Quantity — quality or standard promised.
categoryGates.question: What was wrong with what you received, or how did it fall short of what you expected?

options.label: It didn't meet a quality or specification that was expressly agreed
It fell below the ordinary standard you'd expect for that kind of good or service
There was no quality problem

categoryGates.plainExplanation: Even without an express quality clause, the law implies goods must be of satisfactory quality and services performed with reasonable care and skill.
categoryGates.missingMessage: What exactly was wrong with what you received, compared with what you expected?
categoryGates.exceptions: If goods were sold explicitly 'as-is', or defects were pointed out and accepted, quality obligations may be excluded or limited — check for this.

source.title: Sale of Goods Act 1979; common law
source.provision: s 14 (satisfactory quality, fitness for purpose); duty of reasonable care and skill for services

categoryGates.description: Quality & Quantity — quantity or scope agreed.
categoryGates.question: Was a specific quantity of goods, or scope of service, agreed?

options.label: Yes — and what I received fell short of it
Yes — and it was delivered in full
No specific quantity or scope was agreed

categoryGates.plainExplanation: Establishes the measurable scope of performance, needed to quantify damages later. Without an agreed quantity it is hard to show a shortfall — reframe around quality or completeness instead.
categoryGates.missingMessage: How much or how many were you supposed to get, and how much did you actually receive? Was there a minimum you needed?
categoryGates.exceptions: Partial delivery may still discharge part of the obligation — check whether partial performance was accepted or rejected.

source.title: Sale of Goods Act 1979
source.provision: s 30 (delivery of wrong quantity)

categoryGates.description: Payment Terms — price agreed and any change.
categoryGates.question: Was a clear price agreed at the start?
categoryGates.plainExplanation: A unilateral price change without the other party's consent is generally not enforceable — central to unfair pricing complaints. With no clear original price, you may have to rely on a 'reasonable price'.
categoryGates.missingMessage: Was a price ever explicitly stated or written down? Did the amount you were asked to pay change from what was first discussed?
categoryGates.exceptions: A price increase communicated and accepted (even implicitly, e.g. paying without objection) may bind the claimant; an increase imposed unilaterally without consent may not.

source.title: General contract law; Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act
source.provision: Variation of terms (requires mutual consent); CPFTA unfair practices (B2C)

categoryGates.description: Payment Terms — interest / credit limit. Table: relevant mainly to disputing interest the other side claims. Draft: legal to decide whether to publish.
categoryGates.question: Was any interest rate or late-payment charge agreed?
categoryGates.plainExplanation: Interest is not automatically implied into commercial contracts — it must typically be agreed, or claimed as statutory interest on the judgment sum itself.
categoryGates.missingMessage: Did anyone mention what would happen if payment was late — any extra charges or interest?
categoryGates.exceptions: If no interest rate was agreed, none can generally be claimed unless implied by statute or established trade practice; excessive rates may themselves be challengeable.

source.title: General contract law; Small Claims Tribunals Act
source.provision: Power to award interest on judgment sums, distinct from contractual interest

categoryGates.description: Payment Terms — form of payment. Table: unlikely a standalone issue. Draft.
categoryGates.question: Was a specific form of payment agreed (cash, transfer, cheque, goods-in-kind)?
categoryGates.plainExplanation: Relevant mainly where a dispute arises over refusal of a particular payment form causing delay or breach.
categoryGates.missingMessage: How was payment actually made, or supposed to be made?
categoryGates.exceptions: If no form was specified, any commercially reasonable form is generally acceptable.

source.title: General contract law
source.provision: Implied term of reasonable manner of performance

categoryGates.description: Payment Terms — evidence of payment channel/record.
categoryGates.question: Do you have a bank statement, app transaction record, or receipt showing the payment (or that payment was not made)?
categoryGates.plainExplanation: Largely an evidence-gathering point rather than a distinct legal obligation — it supports proof that payment (or non-payment) occurred. Retrieve bank or payment-app records before filing.
categoryGates.missingMessage: Can you check your bank or payment app for a record of the transaction?

source.title: Evidentiary best practice
source.provision: Not a distinct statutory term

categoryGates.description: Payment Terms — when payment was due.
categoryGates.question: Was a payment due date agreed — upfront, on delivery, or after a credit period such as '30 days from invoice'?
categoryGates.plainExplanation: Establishes exactly when the payment obligation was triggered, needed to assess whether late or non-payment actually constitutes a breach yet.
categoryGates.missingMessage: Was there ever a due date mentioned for payment, or an invoice with payment terms?
categoryGates.exceptions: If unspecified, payment is generally implied due on or around delivery or completion, unless trade practice suggests otherwise.

source.title: Sale of Goods Act 1979
source.provision: s 28 (payment and delivery as concurrent conditions, absent contrary agreement)

categoryGates.description: Conditions Precedent — things the claimant had to do first.
categoryGates.question: Was there anything you had to do first — pay a deposit, provide access or information — before the other side was obliged to deliver or perform? If so, did you do it?

options.label: No — there was nothing I had to do first
Yes — and I did it
Yes — but I did not do it, or not fully

categoryGates.plainExplanation: If you did not meet a condition you had to satisfy first, the other party's non-performance may be excused — this goes to who breached first.
categoryGates.missingMessage: Was there anything you had to do first before the other side would deliver or perform?
categoryGates.exceptions: If the other party waived the condition by their conduct (e.g. proceeding without requiring it), it may no longer be enforceable against you.

source.title: General contract law
source.provision: Conditions precedent and concurrent conditions

categoryGates.description: Conditions Precedent — things the other party had to do first. Draft: this row establishes a point in the claimant's favour rather than a weakness; needs a different severity model or a rephrase. Legal to decide.
categoryGates.question: Was the other party supposed to do or provide anything before you had to pay or accept?
categoryGates.plainExplanation: Conditions the other side had to satisfy first are critical to establishing who actually breached first.
categoryGates.missingMessage: Was the other side supposed to inspect, certify or deliver anything before you were obliged to pay or accept?
categoryGates.exceptions: A buyer accepting goods or services despite an unmet condition may lose the right to rely on it later.

source.title: General contract law
source.provision: Conditions precedent and concurrent conditions

categoryGates.description: Notice Obligations — claimant's notice of the problem.
categoryGates.question: When did you first tell the other party there was a problem?

options.label: Promptly after I discovered the problem
After a significant delay
I have not told them yet

categoryGates.plainExplanation: Timely notice affects whether a defect claim remains open — prolonged silence can be read as having accepted the goods 'as is'.
categoryGates.missingMessage: When did you first raise the problem with the other party, and how — call, message, email?
categoryGates.exceptions: Even without an express notice clause, a buyer who delays too long in complaining about defects may be treated as having accepted the goods.

source.title: Sale of Goods Act 1979; general contract law
source.provision: s 35 (acceptance by lapse of time); notice and waiver

categoryGates.description: Notice Obligations — seller's failure to warn. Table: aggravates a claim rather than weakening it. Draft: needs a different severity model. Legal to decide.
categoryGates.question: Did the other party warn you in advance about any delay or issue, or did you only find out afterwards?
categoryGates.plainExplanation: A seller's failure to give reasonable notice of known problems can aggravate a breach claim or support a separate claim.
categoryGates.missingMessage: Did the other party say anything in advance about a delay or a problem?
categoryGates.exceptions: Silence by a seller who knew of a problem and said nothing may itself support a claim (e.g. misrepresentation by omission in some circumstances).

source.title: General contract law; Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act
source.provision: Non-disclosure as unfair practice (B2C only)

categoryGates.description: Confidentiality. Table: 'likely irrelevant to the claim; skip'. Draft — do not publish unless the demo scenario involves confidential information.
categoryGates.question: Was anything shared between you that was meant to stay private?
categoryGates.plainExplanation: Relevant mainly if the dispute itself involves an alleged breach of confidentiality — not typically central to payment or quality disputes.
categoryGates.missingMessage: Did either side ask the other to keep details of the deal confidential?
categoryGates.exceptions: Confidentiality obligations are rare in simple consumer transactions — mainly relevant in B2B claims involving sensitive information.

source.title: General contract and equity principles
source.provision: Implied confidentiality in certain business relationships

categoryGates.description: Loss Mitigation — both buyer-side and seller-side rows merged into one role-neutral question.
categoryGates.question: After the other party failed to do what was promised, did you take reasonable steps to limit your loss — for example asking for a fix or refund, stopping further payments or work, finding another provider, or reselling goods?
categoryGates.plainExplanation: Your damages can be reduced — though not eliminated — if you failed to take reasonable steps to limit your own loss once the breach became apparent.
categoryGates.missingMessage: After things went wrong, what did you do next — ask for a fix, a refund, stop paying, or find another provider?
categoryGates.exceptions: The duty to mitigate does not require accepting an unreasonable substitute or incurring excessive further cost.

source.title: General contract law
source.provision: Duty to mitigate loss

categoryGates.description: Warranty & Returns — warranty period and timing of defect.
categoryGates.question: Was a warranty period stated, and when did the problem show up relative to purchase?

options.label: Within a stated warranty period
Within 6 months of purchase (no warranty period was stated)
More than 6 months after purchase, and no warranty period was stated

categoryGates.plainExplanation: Warranty periods define the window during which defects are presumed attributable to the seller rather than misuse. Under Singapore's Lemon Law, a defect appearing within 6 months is presumed to have existed at delivery.
categoryGates.missingMessage: Was anything said about how long the product or service was guaranteed for? Roughly when did the problem appear compared with when you bought it?
categoryGates.exceptions: Even without an express warranty, the implied satisfactory-quality obligation covers a reasonable period after purchase.

source.title: Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act; Sale of Goods Act 1979
source.provision: Lemon Law provisions (6-month presumption); SOGA s 14

categoryGates.description: Warranty & Returns — refund/return/exchange conditions and whether a remedy was sought.
categoryGates.question: Did you ask the other party for a repair, replacement, refund or price reduction?
categoryGates.plainExplanation: For defective goods the law sets a remedy hierarchy — repair or replace first, then refund or price reduction. Asking for one of these is usually the first step, and a blanket 'no refunds' sign cannot take these statutory rights away in a consumer sale.
categoryGates.missingMessage: Did you see or agree to any return or refund policy, and have you asked for a refund, repair or replacement?
categoryGates.exceptions: 'No refund' policies do not override a consumer's statutory right to a remedy for non-conforming goods — flag if the business relies purely on a blanket no-refund sign.

source.title: Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act; Sale of Goods Act 1979
source.provision: CPFTA; SOGA ss 48A–48F (remedies for defective goods)

categoryGates.description: Liability & Indemnity — any agreed cap or exclusion. PASS when none is present; WEAKNESS when one is, because it may (or may not) be enforceable.
categoryGates.question: Did any terms, receipt or contract mention limits on what the other party would be responsible for if something went wrong — for example 'liability capped at the price paid'?
categoryGates.plainExplanation: The other party may try to rely on a cap or exclusion. These are often overstated: clauses that exclude liability for statutory implied terms are void or restricted in consumer contracts, though more readily enforceable between businesses if reasonable.
categoryGates.missingMessage: Check any receipt, terms and conditions or contract for wording about limits on the other party's responsibility.
categoryGates.exceptions: Exclusion clauses that try to exclude liability for statutory implied terms are void or restricted in consumer contracts under the Unfair Contract Terms Act; in B2B contracts such clauses are more readily enforceable if reasonable.

source.title: Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977; Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act
source.provision: UCTA 1977 (Singapore); CPFTA

categoryGates.description: Liability & Indemnity — indemnity clause. Table: 'likely irrelevant; skip unless a third-party loss is part of the dispute'. Draft.
categoryGates.question: Did the contract say one side would cover the other's losses if a third party made a claim or something specific went wrong?
categoryGates.plainExplanation: Indemnities shift risk for specific losses beyond ordinary damages — relevant mainly to B2B disputes involving third-party claims.
categoryGates.missingMessage: Did the contract mention anything about one side covering the other's losses?
categoryGates.exceptions: Indemnity clauses are rare in simple consumer transactions.

source.title: General contract law
source.provision: Indemnity as a distinct contractual remedy from damages
